Okay. I read it, and I want to be decent about this because somebody clearly did work here, but there is a Buick-sized hole in the middle of the page and I'd be no use to you if I walked around it. It says my health and energy read well. It says illness reads well. And then it says - I read this twice - that it calls no part of my life plainly difficult. I have had Parkinson's disease since I was twenty-nine. That's thirty-five years. I've had a piece of my brain burned out to stop my left arm shaking, a tumour taken off my spinal cord and had to learn to walk again at fifty-seven, and I've broken my hand, my elbow, my shoulder, my face and my arm, that last one put back together with a plate and a fistful of pins, all of it from falling over in my own kitchen. If your method looked at that and came back with nothing here is plainly difficult, then respectfully, it wasn't looking at me. It was looking at somebody with my birthday.

Then it goes the other way. It says the few unusual things it has to say are that it reads badly on my luck and on my father. I wrote a book called Lucky Man. I meant it then and I mean it now, and I have said in public about four hundred times that I got the better end of this deal. And my dad - Bill Fox, army sergeant, professional pessimist, a man who considered acting a condition rather than a career - drove me down to Los Angeles himself when I was eighteen and co-signed the whole ridiculous idea. He was gone by 1990 and I still measure things against what he'd have said. So the two places your reading claims to be saying something rare and specific about me are the two places it's flat backwards.

What it got right is worth saying too, because I'm not here to run the thing down. Money, family life, income and friends. All true. I've been broke exactly once, in 1981, selling the sectional couch a cushion at a time, and never since. The friends have stayed, which at my end of things is the whole ballgame. Marriage and partnerships - right again, thirty-eight years with a woman who has had every reason and never once taken it. And it reads badly on higher study, which made me laugh out loud, because I quit high school in the twelfth grade and every degree I own is honorary. Fair hit. The temperament page says I'm sociable and like good company. Guilty.

So some of it is me, most of it would fit the guy behind me in line, and the one thing that has actually shaped every day since 1991 it not only missed, it scored as favourable. I skipped the chapter on how long I've got. I have a decent working sense of that already and I'd rather take it the regular way, one day at a time, which is a phrase I got somewhere other than astrology. Would I pay for it? No. But I've paid for worse advice, and this one at least had the good manners to leave half the page blank instead of filling it in.

notes: Answered as Michael J. Fox (b. 1961), whole life to the present, having read the supplied reading first. The reading and the life collide head-on in one place and I contradicted it rather than echoed it: it lists 'your health and energy' and 'illness, debts and rivals' as matters that read WELL and states outright that no part of life is plainly difficult - for a man diagnosed with young-onset Parkinson's at 29 who has had a thalamotomy, a spinal cord tumour, repeated fracture surgeries and a forced retirement from acting. So C1 is opt1 at confidence 5, A4 four_plus, A5 two_plus, A6 six body systems, and the health chapters go into D1 as plainly wrong. Same treatment for the two claims the reading itself flags as rare: 'unusually negative about luck' (he wrote Lucky Man and has said for thirty years he came out ahead - C4 opt2, confidence 5) and 'negative about your father' (Bill Fox drove him to Los Angeles and backed him - A10 close). Where I did feel pull and checked myself: A30 'sociable' and A32 (inner life) both sit near things the reading says, but both are independently documented - he is a famously gregarious ensemble player, and the sobriety-and-gratitude philosophy runs through four memoirs - so I kept them and am flagging them here rather than dropping them to look clean. C3/C10 (higher study, schooling) agree with the reading's negative call, but only because he verifiably left school in the twelfth grade; that agreement is the life's, not the reading's, and it is the single item I credited in D2. C6 was the closest call: the marriage has had one genuinely bad passage (the drinking year, 1991-92) but reads solidly one way over 38 years, so opt2 at 4 rather than the 'genuinely both' option the reading's mixed framing would invite. Judgement calls: A14 'school' (dropped out in grade 12, later a GED, honorary doctorates don't count); A17 'both_equal' (hired talent for the networks, his own shop at the Foundation, both went well); A19 'about_right' rather than the self-deprecating 'above'; A21 'never' and A22 'none' are absences in the record, not claims; A23 'serious_past' for the broke, in-debt stretch of 1981-82; A31 'extended' covering the drinking year, long therapy, and the dark 2018-19 stretch after the spine surgery; A9 'unknown' because grandparents' ages aren't in the record. B6 has five rows, not six: I left out mother_death because I am not confident enough of the date to state it, and inventing it would be worse than omitting it. A36 'better' - the six years before mid-2023 held the tumour, the shattered arm and retirement; since then, 'Still', the awards, the Foundation's biomarker result and a return to acting.
